analysis.investment_thesis: Entero Healthcare fails nearly every quantitative filter I require: P/E of 47.8x (vs. my ceiling of 15x), P/B of 3.15x (vs. my ceiling of 1.5x), and the Graham Number of roughly ₹474 is less than 40% of the current price of ₹1,278. Worse, operating cash flow has been negative in all five years on record — meaning the reported profits are not real cash returns to shareholders.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 30% CAGR (2020–2025) to ₹5,096 Cr, demonstrating genuine scale in pharmaceutical distribution.
Debt/Equity of 0.25 is the one balance-sheet metric within acceptable range after the IPO capital raise.
Operating income inflected sharply positive, rising from ₹23 Cr (2020) to ₹172 Cr (2025) — EBITDA margins are at least moving in the right direction.
key_risks: Persistent negative operating cash flow (0 of 5 years positive; FCF -₹87 Cr in 2025) — accounting profits are not translating into real cash, a cardinal sin for a value investor.
Razor-thin 3.4% operating margins in a commoditised distribution business leave no cushion; any pricing pressure or cost shock erases profitability entirely.
Earnings history disqualifies the company — net losses in 2021 (-₹15 Cr), 2022 (-₹29 Cr), and 2023 (-₹11 Cr) mean there is no five-year record of uninterrupted positive earnings I demand.
red_flags: Graham Number ~₹474 vs. market price ₹1,278 — stock trades at nearly 3× intrinsic value by my formula.
Operating cash flow negative every single year since inception; the business consumes cash rather than generating it.
Negative book equity as recently as 2021 (-₹32 Cr reserves); current equity base is almost entirely IPO proceeds, not retained earnings.
No dividend — a distribution company generating 'profits' but unable to return a single rupee to shareholders confirms the cash-flow problem.
Incorporated only in 2018 — by definition cannot satisfy my minimum 5-year consecutive earnings requirement.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Entero Healthcare is a pharmaceutical distributor incorporated in 2018 that went public, raising sufficient capital to turn its equity positive. On the surface, revenue growth (30.4% CAGR) and a recent surge in reported net profit (₹107 Cr in FY2025) look encouraging. But my analysis begins and ends with balance sheet facts and cash. The Graham Number — computed as √(22.5 × EPS of ~₹24.6 × BVPS of ~₹406) — yields approximately ₹474, meaning the market demands a premium of nearly 170% over intrinsic value. I do not pay premiums; I demand discounts. P/E of 47.8x and P/B of 3.15x are not even in the neighbourhood of acceptability.

The deeper problem is cash. A distribution business should convert working capital into cash predictably. Entero has produced negative operating cash flow in every year since 2020, including -₹77 Cr in FY2025 despite ₹107 Cr of reported net profit. That divergence tells me the business is funding its growth through working capital absorption — growing receivables and inventory that may never fully convert. ROE of only 5.63% on a freshly recapitalised balance sheet is meagre. There is no dividend, no margin of safety, no earnings track record, and no cash. Mr. Market is pricing this as a growth story; I see an unproven, cash-consumptive middleman at a speculative valuation. I will pass.
